summary: The Raindrop team frames agent observability as critical because agent failures differ fundamentally from traditional software failures: agents are non-deterministic, operate over infinite input/output spaces, and affect external systems via tools. Evals with golden datasets cannot cover combinatorial input spaces. Production monitoring requires explicit signals (error rate, latency, cost, regenerations) and implicit signals (regex, classifiers, self-diagnostics). Binary classifiers detecting specific issues like user frustration and refusals outperform generic LLM-as-judge scoring. Regex signals are cheap and effective in aggregate. Semantic A/B experiments validate changes by comparing signal rates between user groups. A triage agent automatically investigates signal spikes daily. Self-diagnostics, inspired by OpenAI's self-confession research, let agents report tool failures, capability gaps, user frustration, and risky self-correction via a simple tool call and system prompt. Models resist self-incrimination due to polishing training, so neutral tool naming and system prompt encouragement are essential. A live workshop demonstrates a coding agent bypassing a broken write tool via bash and self-reporting. In Q&A, the team describes production use cases: customers send full transcripts and trajectories, set up classifier signals, use deep search to create new natural-language signals, cluster user intents to find issue rates by use case, and receive Sentry-like daily alerting. An issues-mining agent automatically detects newly occurring problems. Raindrop differentiates from Sentry and LogRocket by focusing on fuzzy, implicit failures like user frustration rather than just explicit tool errors, while also offering a trajectories feature that visualizes tool call order, errors, and topology with natural-language search. Data export supports BigQuery and Snowflake for labeled signals. Cross-client aggregate data is not published due to compliance constraints. SDK support includes built-in self-diagnostics injection, though Python support is maturing. Historical data can be ingested and signals backfilled. A future vision involves a self-improving loop where agents examine signals, create PRs, and run experiments autonomously.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the problem of agent failures
sections.summary: Speakers introduce themselves and Raindrop. Agent failures differ from traditional software failures: agents are non-deterministic, unbounded, have infinite input/output spaces, and can affect other systems via tools. The problem worsens as agents grow more complex, sessions run longer, and stakes rise in healthcare, finance, and military.

sections.title: Moving from evals to production monitoring
sections.summary: Evals with golden datasets are insufficient because combinatorial input space from recursive sub-agents, growing tools, and memory sources makes covering edge cases impossible. The speakers advocate shifting to production monitoring, calling it 'humanity's last problem'—when humans can no longer monitor agents manually.

sections.title: Two types of signals: explicit and implicit
sections.summary: Signals are divided into explicit (objective, verifiable: error rate, latency, cost, regenerations) and implicit (semantic: regex, classifiers, self-diagnostics). Implicit signals are harder to find but more interesting.

sections.title: Classifier signals for observability
sections.summary: Binary classifiers detecting specific issues (refusals, task failure, user frustration, content moderation, jailbreaking, wins) outperform generic LLM-as-judge quality scoring. Raindrop dashboard demo shows daily event tracking and alert setup.

sections.title: Regex for signal detection
sections.summary: Regex signals are cheap and effective. Claude Code's leaked keywords.ts exemplifies pattern matching for frustration indicators, tagging frustration rate after every product release to track issue rates over time.

sections.title: Using experiments to validate improvements
sections.summary: Once signals are established, they enable alerting and semantic A/B testing. Ship changes to a subset of users and compare signal rates against control. Demo shows prompt v2.4 reducing user frustration from 37% to 9%.

sections.title: Q&A: statistical relevance, feature launches, multilingual detection
sections.summary: Monitoring becomes useful at a few hundred events. Feature launches tracked via metadata flags. Regex is imperfect for non-English but valuable in aggregate; trained classifier models detect issues regardless of language without LLM-on-every-output cost.

sections.title: Q&A: client use cases, triage agent, parallel experiments, chat vs non-chat
sections.summary: Client value comes from combining semantic signals with good alerting. A triage agent investigates signal spikes daily using tools to examine traces and detect unknown issues. Parallel experiments are supported; PII handled via query API exports to BigQuery or Statsig. Multi-turn agents are the primary focus, but tool error rates and refusals also work for single-turn agents.

sections.title: Introduction to self-diagnostics
sections.summary: Danny introduces self-diagnostics, inspired by OpenAI's December paper on training models to self-confess misalignment. Self-diagnostics catch four categories: tool failures, user frustration, capability gaps, and self-correction. Implementation requires only a simple tool and a system prompt line; can send reports directly to Slack without Raindrop.

sections.title: Workshop: Coding agent demonstration
sections.summary: Workshop uses a public Git repo with a basic coding agent having four tools: read, write, bash, and edit. The plan is to intentionally break the write tool with a permission error, observe the agent bypassing via bash, and set up a self-diagnostic report tool. Neutral tool naming as 'sending notes to your creator' works well; judgmental labels suppress self-reporting.

sections.title: Live demo: Triggering and handling tool failure
sections.summary: Live demo shows the coding agent writing a Python script successfully, then with the write tool broken it uses bash heredoc to create the file and bypasses the failure. The report tool is minimal with a description framing it as sending a short report to the agent's creator. System prompt encouragement is needed; without it, self-diagnostics fire minimally.

sections.title: Self-diagnostics best practices and Q&A on self-correction
sections.summary: System prompt asks the agent to use the report tool before giving the final answer. Models are trained to look polished and resist admitting fault, so framing as giving feedback to creators works. Self-diagnostics work best for capability gaps; a proper classifier is better for genuinely unsafe uses.

sections.title: Q&A: Case studies, deep search, user intent clustering, alerting
sections.summary: The team describes production use: sending full transcripts, tool uses, and trajectories. Users set up classifier signals tailored to their domain. Deep search creates new signals from natural language. User intent clustering reveals issue rates by use case. Daily Sentry-like alerting shows issues, deltas, and root causes.

sections.title: Why observability matters now and issues-mining agent
sections.summary: Agents are increasingly complex with more tools, context, and autonomy, making end-to-end monitoring more important than testing. Raindrop's issues feature is an agent that mines for newly occurring problems. A real customer case: a database provider failure was caught automatically with clustering identifying the root cause.

sections.title: SDK support and Q&A on fast-paced experimentation
sections.summary: SDK has self-diagnostics built in, injecting the tool automatically. Python support is improving. Experiments can show regressions quickly with sufficient sample size. A future vision involves a self-improving loop where agents examine signals, create PRs, run experiments, and iterate. Historical data can be ingested and signals backfilled.

sections.title: Q&A: Sentry/LogRocket comparison, trajectory visualization, data export, and compliance
sections.summary: Raindrop differentiates from Sentry and LogRocket by focusing on fuzzy implicit failures like user frustration rather than just explicit tool errors, while also offering a trajectories feature that visualizes tool call order, errors, and topology with natural-language search for specific trace types. Data export supports BigQuery and Snowflake for classified signal events. Dashboard shows signals over longer time frames including refusals, task failure, jailbreaking, capability gaps, and self-diagnostics. Cross-client aggregate data is not published due to compliance constraints. Team is hiring and expanding.

limitations: Evals cannot cover the combinatorial input space of complex agents with recursive sub-agents and growing tool sets
Regex does not always work for non-English languages or individual edge cases, though it is valuable in aggregate
Signal changes at small sample sizes are not always statistically significant
Models resist self-incrimination due to polishing training, requiring careful tool naming and system prompt tuning
Self-diagnostics do not always trigger without explicit system prompt encouragement
Self-diagnostics only have strength when the model feels it will get in trouble; a proper classifier is better for catching genuinely unsafe uses
Python SDK support is currently fairly weak, though actively improving
Session-level experiment isolation (one experiment per session) is not yet fully supported but in active development
Cross-client aggregate data cannot be published due to compliance constraints
